opus-5.5.text:
I think of it as a partnership where each side covers the other's weaknesses. Language models are remarkably good at the creative, intuitive part of mathematics: guessing which lemma might be useful, suggesting a proof strategy, recognizing that a problem resembles something from a different field. That's the part that has always felt most "human" about math. But they are also unreliable. They can write something that looks like a beautiful proof and has a subtle gap in step seven, and in mathematics a proof that's 99% correct is simply not a proof.

Formal verification tools, like Lean, are the opposite. They have no intuition at all, but they are completely rigorous. If Lean accepts your proof, it's correct, full stop. So the natural design is to let the model propose and let the verifier dispose. The model generates candidate proofs or proof steps in a formal language, the verifier checks them, and the feedback, whether it's an error message, an unsolved goal, or a success, goes back to the model. That loop becomes a very clean learning signal. Unlike many other domains, you don't need a human grader or a fuzzy reward model. You have ground truth.

A few things make this harder than it sounds, though. One is autoformalization, which means translating a problem or a proof written in ordinary mathematical language into a formal statement that faithfully captures what was meant. If you formalize the statement slightly wrong, you can verify a perfect proof of the wrong theorem. So I think a lot of the real work sits at that interface between informal and formal math.

Another is data. Formal mathematics libraries are tiny compared to the internet's worth of informal math. So you want the system to generate its own training data: propose conjectures, attempt proofs, keep what verifies, and gradually grow both its own capability and the library itself. That self-improving loop is, to me, one of the most exciting parts of the whole field.

And finally, I don't think the goal is just a theorem-proving machine. The ideal system works with mathematicians. It handles the tedious verification and the search, and it might surface surprising connections, while humans bring taste: deciding which questions are actually interesting and worth asking. If we get the combination right, the language model gives you imagination, the verifier gives you trust, and together you get something that can do mathematics at a scale and with a reliability we haven't had before.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I think the honest answer is that they are good at opposite things, and the whole design question is how to make the division of labor work.

Language models are good at intuition. They can read a problem, guess which lemma matters, propose a decomposition, and produce something that looks like a proof. But "looks like" is the problem. A model can write ten pages of fluent mathematics with a subtle gap on page three, and no human reviewer wants to be the one who finds it. The model doesn't know when it's wrong, and it doesn't know that it doesn't know.

Formal verification tools, Lean in particular, are the opposite. They have no intuition at all. They won't suggest anything. But if a proof type-checks, it is correct, full stop. There's no "I'm pretty sure." That's an incredibly rare property in machine learning. Almost everything else we build is probabilistic, and here is a component that gives you a hard guarantee.

So the way I think about the system is: the language model proposes, the verifier disposes. The model generates candidate proof steps, Lean checks each one, and the failure comes back as a signal. The important thing is that the verifier isn't just a filter at the end. It's inside the loop. When a tactic fails, the error message is information, and you feed it back so the model can revise. That turns proving into something closer to search with a perfect oracle, which is a much better problem than "generate text and hope."

The second thing it gives you is training data you can trust. If you're doing reinforcement learning, your reward is only as good as your ability to judge outcomes. In most domains that judgment is a human or another model, both of which are noisy and gameable. In formal math the reward is just "did it compile." You can't reward-hack a type checker. That means you can let the system generate millions of attempts, keep the verified ones, and improve on them without the whole thing drifting into confident nonsense.

What I don't think works is treating formalization as an afterthought, where the model does informal math and then someone translates. Autoformalization is hard, and it's where a lot of errors creep in, because the statement you prove might not be the statement you meant. So the model has to be fluent in the formal language natively. The informal reasoning is still valuable, it's the scaffolding, but the thing that gets checked has to be the thing the model actually produced.

The long-term version is a system where mathematicians interact in natural language, the model handles the tedious formal work underneath, and every result that comes out is machine-verified. That changes what collaboration in math looks like, because you can trust a result from someone, or something, without re-deriving it yourself. That's really the goal: not replacing mathematicians, but removing the bottleneck of verification so human creativity can go further.

astra-6.text:
I think they play complementary roles. The language model can propose ideas: a useful lemma, a proof strategy, or a connection between two problems. The formal-verification tool then checks whether the proposed argument actually follows from the definitions and assumptions.

The interesting part is making that a feedback loop. Rather than asking a model to generate an entire proof and checking it only at the end, you let it work through intermediate steps. The verifier tells it what remains to be proved or where a step fails, and the model uses that information to revise its approach.

But verification doesn’t remove every source of error. You still have to make sure that the formal statement captures the mathematical question you intended to ask. A perfectly verified proof of the wrong statement doesn’t solve your problem.

So I’d want a system where the model has room to explore, the verifier provides a precise standard of correctness, and the resulting proof is also explained in a way that helps a human understand why it works.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they play complementary roles. A language model is good at proposing ideas: spotting a pattern, suggesting a useful lemma, or sketching a possible proof. A formal-verification tool can then check whether those steps actually follow from the assumptions.

The interesting part is making that a feedback loop. The model proposes a proof, the verifier identifies gaps or errors, and the model uses that feedback to revise its approach. Sometimes the missing piece is a small technical step; sometimes it means the whole strategy needs to change.

But checking a proof and discovering a useful proof are different problems. You still need a system that can choose promising intermediate statements and search at the right level of abstraction. So I’d want the language model to guide that exploration, with formal verification providing a precise standard for what counts as a completed proof.
